bodyHtml:
API 510 in one paragraph: the current edition, checked against the code

API 510 is the American Petroleum Institute's in-service inspection code for pressure vessels and the pressure-relieving devices that protect them. It covers inspection, repair, alteration and rerating after a vessel enters service. The current edition is the eleventh, published in October 2022. API's announcement says the edition updates the in-service and condition-monitoring programs and adds a detailed section on analysing inspection results. It is written for the hydrocarbon and chemical process industries, but an owner-operator may choose to apply it to process vessels in other industries.

This section restates the essentials from the eleventh edition in plain language, with clause references where we checked them. Several figures that circulate online, including some earlier in this guide, describe earlier editions or third-party practice rather than the code. Where this section and the material above differ, rely on this section and on your licensed copy of the code. API codes are copyrighted, so this is a summary, not a substitute for the standard.

Which vessels API 510 covers, and which it excludes

API 510 applies to process vessels that have been placed in service, unless they are specifically excluded. That includes vessels built to a construction code such as the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, vessels built without any code, jurisdictional-special vessels, and nonstandard vessels whose nameplate or stamping has been lost. For ASME Section VIII construction, the eleventh edition says API 510 is intended for Divisions 1 and 2, not Division 3.

The code also draws lines that matter in practice:

  • Decommissioned versus idle. Vessels that have been officially decommissioned, meaning they are no longer an asset of record, fall outside the code. Abandoned-in-place vessels may still need some inspection so they do not become a hazard, and vessels that are temporarily out of service and preserved for future use remain covered.
  • Exclusions in Annex A. The excluded classes are listed in an annex. They broadly include vessels on movable structures covered by other regulations (such as vessels on ships, barges and trucks), classes of containers exempted from the scope of ASME Section VIII Division 1, and very small vessels below volume and pressure thresholds. The owner-operator may still choose to include any excluded vessel in its program. The eleventh edition suggests that some vessels exempt under Section VIII Division 1, such as large vacuum vessels, be considered for inclusion based on risk.
  • Exploration and production vessels. Vessels in drilling, production, gathering, transport and treatment of oil, gas, NGL and brine may be inspected under alternative rules in Section 9 instead of Section 6, while every other section still applies.
  • Source inspection is out of scope. API 510 does not cover source inspection of newly fabricated vessels. The code points to API RP 588 for supplier surveillance.

Where API 510 and the construction code both address an in-service vessel, or conflict, API 510 takes precedence. Where a regulation applies, API 510 cannot be used to conflict with it, but if API 510 is more stringent, its requirements govern. That is why a site can work to API 510 and a state or provincial law at the same time.

Who does what under API 510

API 510 is built around defined roles. Its intent clause says the code is for owner-operators that employ or have access to an authorized inspection agency, a repair organization, an engineer, an inspector and examiners. Getting these roles right answers most practical questions about who can sign what.

RoleWhat API 510 expects (paraphrased, 11th edition Section 4)
Owner-operatorOwns the program: quality assurance system, inspection plans, records, management of change, and responding to inspection findings that need corrective action.
Inspector (API 510 authorized pressure vessel inspector)Responsible to the owner-operator for making sure inspection, NDE, repairs, alterations and pressure tests meet the code. Directly involved in inspection, especially visual work. Evaluates and accepts all NDE results and makes recommendations. Certified under the code's Annex B; may be an employee or an acceptable contractor.
ExaminerPerforms NDE to the job requirements, NDE procedures and owner specifications. Does not need API 510 certification and need not be an owner employee, but must be trained and competent in the procedures used. Owners may require certifications such as ASNT SNT-TC-1A, ASNT CP-189, CGSB or AWS QC1.
EngineerHandles engineering evaluations such as rerating, repair design and assessments of damage.
Repair organizationPerforms repairs and alterations under the code's requirements.

The examiner row answers a common misconception. API 510 certification is not required to perform UT, MT, PT, RT or advanced NDE on a vessel. It is required of the inspector who evaluates the results. The code also says the examiner's employer must keep certification records and make them available to the inspector, who confirms the examiners are qualified for their work. That is the boundary Atlantis works within: we supply the examiners and Level III procedure support, and the owner's API 510 inspector remains inspector of record.

The interval ceilings, stated correctly

API 510 sets ceilings; the inspector or engineer sets the actual interval under the owner-operator's quality assurance system. In the eleventh edition, unless an RBI assessment justifies otherwise, the default ceilings are:

  • External visual inspection: at least every five years, or sooner if the internal/on-stream interval is shorter, preferably with the vessel operating (6.4.1). There is no annual external requirement in the code; any annual rounds are owner or jurisdiction practice.
  • Internal or on-stream inspection: no longer than half the remaining life or 10 years, whichever is less. When remaining life is under four years, the interval may be the full remaining life up to two years (6.5.1.1).
  • Thickness-measurement inspections: the same half-remaining-life-or-10-years ceiling (6.5.1.2).
  • Pressure-relieving devices: unless documented experience or RBI supports longer, intervals should not exceed five years in typical process service and 10 years in clean, non-fouling, non-corrosive service (6.6.3.2).
  • RBI: an RBI assessment complying with API RP 580 may set intervals beyond those limits; in the eleventh edition RBI external intervals may not exceed 10 years, and RBI internal/on-stream intervals over 10 years need engineer and inspector review at least every 10 years (6.3).

On-stream inspection can stand in for an internal inspection only where entry is impossible or a list of conditions is met. Those conditions include a low known general corrosion rate, remaining life above 10 years, an established service history, no environmental cracking or hydrogen damage, and no loose liner. Our guide to API 510 intervals in wet H2S service shows how that condition plays out in sour service. The eleventh edition also formalises deferrals: a short simplified deferral (no more than 10% of the interval or six months, whichever is less, once) and a risk-assessed deferral for anything longer, all documented.

What changed across recent editions

Most people asking about the "api 510 publication" want to know which edition is current and what changed. The ninth edition was published in 2006. Its public copy is still easy to find online, but it is superseded and should not be used to cite current requirements. A tenth edition came in between. The eleventh edition, October 2022, is current, with Errata 1 (March 2023) and Errata 2 (2025) according to publisher listings.

Comparing the 2006 and 2022 texts at a high level:

TopicNinth edition (2006)Eleventh edition (2022)
Scope wordingRefining and chemical process vesselsHydrocarbon and chemical process vessels; may be applied in other industries at owner discretion; explicit treatment of decommissioned, abandoned and preserved vessels
Interval ceilingsFive-year external, half remaining life or 10 years internal/on-streamSame ceilings, plus separate thickness-measurement ceiling and an exemption route when a corrosion SME documents no credible internal mechanisms
RBIAllowed to set intervals, with review over 10 yearsMust comply with API RP 580; RBI external intervals capped at 10 years; PRD intervals included
DeferralsNot structuredFormal deferral rules for inspections and for repair recommendations
Damage mechanismsReferenced generallyExplicit list by damage category with API RP 571 references; inspection plans must cover each credible mechanism
Recognised assessment methodsFFS and RBI recognisedAPI 579-1/ASME FFS-1, API RP 580 and API RP 581 named

Treat this as orientation, not a complete change list. API's ICP publications effectivity sheet tells you which edition and errata apply to each certification exam window, and your site procedures should state the edition your program works to.

Companion documents API 510 relies on

API 510 is short on technique and long on cross-references. The API 510 inspector body of knowledge published by API's certification program includes API RP 571 (damage mechanisms), RP 572 (pressure vessel inspection practices), RP 576 (pressure-relieving devices), RP 577 (welding inspection and metallurgy) and RP 578 (material verification), along with ASME Section V (NDE methods), Section VIII Division 1 (design), Section IX (welding qualification) and ASME PCC-2 (repair methods).

In practice: API RP 571 tells you what damage to expect, RP 572 tells you how vessels are usually inspected, and ASME Section V governs how the NDE is performed. API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 is the reference for fitness-for-service assessment, and API RP 580/581 for risk-based inspection. FFS and RBI are engineering assessments the owner commissions from qualified engineers. Atlantis does not perform them. See the API 571 overview and the API 580 overview.

Where API 510 becomes a legal requirement

API 510 is a voluntary industry code until someone adopts it, and in North America several authorities do. Federally, BSEE's offshore production safety rule (30 CFR 250.851) requires pressure and fired vessels on Outer Continental Shelf production facilities to be repaired, maintained and inspected in accordance with API 510. OSHA's process safety management standard (29 CFR 1910.119(j)) requires mechanical integrity inspections to follow recognised and generally accepted good engineering practice, and API 510 is the usual practice for refinery and chemical process vessels.

At state level, many jurisdictions regulate unfired pressure vessels through boiler and pressure vessel programs that reference the National Board Inspection Code, and some recognise owner-user inspection programs. See API 510 vs the NBIC commissioned inspector. In Canada, pressure equipment is regulated provincially, for example by ABSA in Alberta and TSSA in Ontario, and API 510 is commonly used inside approved owner-user programs. Requirements vary, so confirm with your jurisdiction.

API 510 certification: the published facts

API 510 the code and API 510 the certification are related but different things. The certification is run by API's Individual Certification Programs. According to API's certification page, eligibility combines education with experience: one year of inspection supervision or performance for a degree in engineering or technology, and two, three or five or more years of pressure vessel design, fabrication, repair, operation or inspection for lower education tiers, with at least one year in inspection in each case. ASNT Level III certification is not a prerequisite.

API describes the exam as a 7.5-hour sitting with 170 questions (140 scored), split into closed-book and open-book portions, delivered at Prometric test centres. Certification lasts three years. Recertification requires inspection work over the cycle, 24 CPD hours, and a web quiz every six years. API publishes exam fees and testing windows on its Schedules and Fees page; check there for current figures and dates. For more, see API 510 certification, the API exam schedule and the 2026 body of knowledge changes. Atlantis does not provide API certification training. For people building inspection experience, ASNT NDT qualification is the complementary path; see NDT Level II training.

How Atlantis supports API 510 programs

Atlantis performs the NDE that API 510 inspection plans require: UT thickness and CML surveys, corrosion mapping, phased array and TOFD weld examination, MT, PT, VT, ET and radiography by crews licensed where the work is. Our technicians are ASNT-certified and work under ASNT Level III oversight. We deliver results to the owner's API 510 inspector, who remains inspector of record and sets intervals. We do not act as the authorized inspection agency and do not perform RBI or FFS. See pressure vessel inspection services. Quotes are returned within 24 hours: request a quote for API 510 vessel NDE.

More questions about API 510

What is the current edition of API 510?

The eleventh edition, published October 2022, with Errata 1 (2023) and Errata 2 (2025). Check API's publication listing and the ICP effectivity sheet for the version that applies to your program or exam window.

Does API 510 cover ASME Section VIII Division 3 vessels?

No. The eleventh edition says that for vessels built to ASME Section VIII, API 510 is intended for Divisions 1 and 2, not Division 3.

How often does API 510 require an external inspection?

At least every five years, or at the internal/on-stream interval if that is shorter, unless an RBI assessment justifies otherwise; under RBI the external interval may not exceed 10 years. The code does not require annual external inspections.

Do NDE technicians need API 510 certification?

No. API 510 says examiners do not need API 510 inspector certification but must be trained and competent in the NDE procedures they use. Owners commonly require ASNT SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 certification.

Is API 510 mandatory?

It is a voluntary industry code that becomes mandatory where adopted, for example by BSEE in 30 CFR 250.851 for offshore production vessels, or through state and provincial rules. Under OSHA PSM it is the usual recognised practice for process vessels.

What does API 510 not cover?

Piping (API 570), atmospheric storage tanks (API 653), source inspection of new vessels (API RP 588), decommissioned vessels, and the excluded classes in its Annex A, such as vessels on movable structures and very small vessels.
